title: Black Basta historical investigation with May and November publication IOC coverage
description: VERSION 2; historical IOC matching exercise, not one documented victim. Retains v1's fictional November-based 23-step story and explicitly adds the original May 10, 2024 publication Tables 7–11 as historical coverage observations. Source sets remain separately identified in catalogs/intelligence/aa24-131a-publication-coverage-v2.json. The six November replacement indicators remain represented; the superseded May indicators are included deliberately for offline historical matching, not asserted currently malicious. Supplemental observations on Windows/Linux hosts are authored independent matching fixtures, not a claim that every affiliate, binary, address, or domain occurred in one intrusion. DNS answers are NXDOMAIN; no source IP/domain resolution is inferred. Source hashes describe synthetic metadata only; no malware is downloaded, executed or generated. Exact digests, canonical paths, IPs and domains are retained from the publication, with documented de-fanging/whitespace/case/path-pattern normalization. Unspecified sample filenames, host placement, timing, counts, privileges, ports, byte totals, benign comparison and containment remain fictional. Commands are inert strings. Recommended run: seed 2; 23 hosts; 2024-11-12T08:00:00Z; 120 minutes; 10000 total events; a NEW output directory. Requires the hash-field support added with v2. Only this scenario JSON is a generation input; the companion catalog checks coverage after export. Full details and limits: docs/examples/aa24-131a-black-basta-v2-notes.md. STIX attachment/consumer CSV parity is unverified because those bytes were unavailable; coverage here is explicitly against the published tables.

steps.description: DOCUMENTED: p.3 lists PrintNightmare CVE-2021-34527 (CWE-269) among privilege escalation weaknesses reported for affiliates. FICTIONAL: an assessment flags dc-01 as unpatched; no exploitation of this CVE is asserted in this branch. Seed 2 yields Windows Server 2019 on dc-01. This contextual finding is independent of the selected social-engineering entry path; a scanner claim alone does not establish exploitability.

DOCUMENTED: pp.4-5 caution that legitimate tools alone are not malicious. FICTIONAL BENIGN CONTROL: an approved svc_backup session runs Rclone on prod-file-02 and transfers data to the pre-existing authorized backup provider. This is a comparison case, not an attack stage.

DOCUMENTED: pp.2-3 and Table 1 describe email bombing followed by fake IT support through calls/Teams, and user execution of AnyDesk or Quick Assist (T1566.004, T1204). FICTIONAL: LAB\operator on prod-rdp-01 accepts an AnyDesk session. The email flood and Teams conversation are narrative prerequisites only; no email/Teams or consent telemetry is emitted. This branch uses AnyDesk, not a ScreenConnect exploit.

DOCUMENTED: Table 8 (p.7) lists Moereng[.]com and Exckicks[.]com as suspected Black Basta Cobalt Strike domains. FICTIONAL: this host queries both and receives NXDOMAIN. No domain-to-IP mapping is invented, and these DNS results are not a historical claim about the domains.

DOCUMENTED: Table 7 (p.6) lists 170.130.165[.]73 as likely Cobalt Strike infrastructure, first seen 2024-10-14. FICTIONAL: an allowed TLS-sized flow from prod-rdp-01 to that historical IP on TCP/443. Neither the port nor flow sizes are source facts; this flow alone does not prove Cobalt Strike.

SOURCE: May Tables 8, 10 and 11. FICTIONAL COVERAGE: original domain strings appear as DNS queries from prod-rdp-01 with NXDOMAIN answers, independently of v1 domain queries. These are matching fixtures; they do not establish a successful callback, real resolution, or current maliciousness. Leading-dot suffixes are represented by an apex query only; suffix scope remains in the catalog.

SOURCE: May Table 8. FICTIONAL COVERAGE: bounded network metadata to each original address. No source ownership, C2 protocol, domain resolution or maliciousness is established; some destinations are shared infrastructure. These independent observations supplement the exercise rather than reconstruct one victim.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Table 1 name SoftPerfect netscan.exe for discovery. FICTIONAL: the utility scans three named assets and five inventory-declared TCP services. Allowed flows show visibility, not completion of LDAP/SMB enumeration.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Table 4 describe discovery utilities with innocuous Intel or Dell names in C:\ (T1036). FICTIONAL: C:\Intel.exe runs on prod-rdp-01; its exact binary, path suffix, parentage and identity are authored. Filename alone does not identify the executable.

DOCUMENTED: Table 7 lists 45.11.181[.]44 as likely Cobalt Strike infrastructure, first seen 2024-10-24. FICTIONAL: a second connection from the same host; distinct addresses are combined for IOC correlation practice and are not asserted to belong to one real intrusion.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Table 1 identify Mimikatz for credential access associated with privilege escalation. FICTIONAL: operator has local administrator rights on this RDP host and elevated remote support has delivered the tool; neither local rights nor successful secret recovery is modeled by the compiler. The subsequent LAB\admin use is an explicit authored outcome, not something established by the process observation.

DOCUMENTED: p.2 reports valid-account abuse; p.3 describes credential access. FICTIONAL: the actor obtains LAB\admin credentials in the preceding gap and authenticates from the RDP host to dc-01 over SMB. This chosen privilege path does not exploit the contextual PrintNightmare finding.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Table 1 report PsExec-assisted lateral movement. FICTIONAL: LAB\admin uses PsExec to execute on prod-file-01. PSEXESVC and a cmd.exe child represent authored service/process visibility. SYSTEM is the well-known local service identity; it is not an added domain account.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 names RDP as another lateral movement mechanism. FICTIONAL: admin connects from prod-rdp-01 to prod-file-02. This is an additional composite branch, not evidence that every affiliate used both RDP and PsExec.

DOCUMENTED: Table 7 lists 79.132.130[.]211 as likely Cobalt Strike infrastructure, first seen 2024-10-24. FICTIONAL: prod-file-01 reaches this historical indicator on TCP/443 after lateral execution. A Cobalt Strike beacon's memory behavior, configuration and protocol are not represented.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Tables 4-5 report PowerShell used to disable antivirus (T1059.001, T1562.001). FICTIONAL: an admin runs an assumed delivered maintenance.ps1 on prod-file-01. Script contents and AV state are absent, so analyst events establish a process launch only, not successful impairment.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Table 4 name Backstab as an EDR-disabling tool. FICTIONAL: backstab.exe launches as admin on prod-file-01 after delivery through remote administration. The path and basename are authored representations of the named software, not file IOCs. No successful EDR shutdown or sensor coverage loss is asserted; telemetry continues.

SOURCE: May Table 7. FICTIONAL COVERAGE: file-creation metadata carrying each published sample SHA-256. Windows EXE/DLL/tool samples use prod-file-01; ELF samples use Linux prod-app-01 with the generic endpoint-lab source. Generic sample names are invented where the report gives only a type. Presence is metadata, not execution, infection success, or real malware bytes.

SOURCE: May Table 9. FICTIONAL COVERAGE: original paths and accompanying hashes appear in file metadata. PDF wrap whitespace in hash tokens is removed; {redacted} path components are replaced with a fictional host/label and matched as wildcard patterns. Relative names are placed beneath a fictional directory. Repeated paths with different hashes are independent sample observations, not an asserted sequence of actual overwrites. No binaries or documents are written to those paths.

DOCUMENTED: pp.2-3 describe theft before encryption; specific victims/files are not provided here. FICTIONAL: LAB\admin reads three invented business files on prod-file-01. Audit policy is assumed enabled. Paths, users and a temporal join support collection investigation but contain no file contents or patient data.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Table 1 report Rclone-assisted exfiltration before encryption. FICTIONAL: admin starts Rclone with an invented remote configuration name. No credentials, runnable payloads or actual transfer are included. V2 HISTORICAL EXERCISE: the process_hash is the original May Table 7 rclone.exe digest, deliberately combined with the November-based fictional chain; not a claim that this binary appeared with those November IPs.

DOCUMENTED: Table 7 identifies 66.42.118[.]54 as an exfiltration server, first seen 2024-10-15. FICTIONAL: two sensors observe one TLS-sized transfer of 2400000 outbound bytes from prod-file-01 to TCP/443 at this historical IP. The two records are two views of one transfer, not two exfiltrations. Rclone-to-destination association and which file bytes moved are not proven by these fields.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 and Table 6 report vssadmin.exe used to delete volume shadow copies (T1490). FICTIONAL: this command line is an authored process observation under admin after the transfer; execution success and backup availability are not modeled.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 reports encryption by Black Basta (T1486). FICTIONAL: a file named wup.exe is delivered through the already established remote administration path and launched on prod-file-01. This filename/path is invented, no hash or malware bytes are supplied, and it is not a published IOC.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 describes .basta or random extensions and ChaCha20/RSA-4096 encryption. FICTIONAL: filesystem observations show the three invented documents with .basta suffixes; process attribution is authored. Extension creation does not establish encryption, cryptographic algorithm, file entropy, or inability to recover.

DOCUMENTED: p.3 names readme.txt; p.2 describes a unique code, .onion contact and a typical 10-12 day payment window. FICTIONAL: readme.txt appears on prod-file-01. Only filename metadata is emitted; no ransom text, onion connection, demand, data leak, payment or actual service outage is simulated.

FICTIONAL RESPONSE EXTENSION: an investigator changes the egress rule and a later retry to the historical exfiltration indicator is blocked. This step is not a CISA-reported response outcome. Rule deployment itself and eradication are not modeled; this is one observed blocked flow, not proof of complete containment, recovery or prevention of earlier theft.
